issues.title: fix: honor WG and AWG site split tunneling
issues.body:
## Summary

Fix WG/AWG site split tunneling when AllowedIPs are IPv4-only, reordered, duplicated or formatted differently. This is the profile-eligibility/route-serialization part extracted from #3030.

Fixes #3375.
Tracking issue: #3378.

## Problem

I found two decisions that could silently defeat the selected site-routing mode:

- `VpnConnection` required both IPv4 and IPv6 default routes, disabling site splitting for valid IPv4-only profiles.
- `LocalSocketController` compared AllowedIPs against one exact two-element array. In sites-only mode, an IPv4-only or reordered default list could therefore bypass the site allowlist and produce a full tunnel.

The custom-route branch also marked IPv6 prefixes as IPv4.

## Changes

- Normalize AllowedIPs from JSON arrays, strings and native configuration text, independent of comma spacing.
- Allow the currently IPv4-based site list when the profile contains `0.0.0.0/0`.
- Honor the site allowlist independently of default-route order, duplicates or IPv6 presence.
- Preserve restricted native AllowedIPs and the original address-family coverage in all-sites/exclusion modes.
- Use `IPAddress` for canonical prefix/address-family serialization and deduplicate generated ranges.
- Add isolated LocalSocketController regression tests and register them in the Windows CMake test suite.

Application-exclusion settings are passed through unchanged. This does not implement Windows application allowlist support. The existing frontend fallback from an empty selected site list to all-sites mode is unchanged.

## Verification

On Windows x64 with Qt 6.10.1 and MSVC 19.53, I compiled the actual controller and regression tests from this standalone branch on dev `3f6ecacf`:

- Before: **36 passed, 26 failed**.
- After: **62 passed, 0 failed** (60 data cases plus setup/cleanup).
- 42 route-generation cases: both protocols, all three site modes, empty/IPv4-only/ordered/reordered/duplicated defaults, restricted routes and default-plus-specific routes.
- 18 application-passthrough cases: both protocols and all site modes, with application splitting disabled, enabled-empty or enabled-populated.

The tests capture activation JSON through an isolated local socket; they do not contact the real service or change routes. These results validate serialization, not end-to-end VPN traffic. I have not switched my live connection to sites-only mode, and have not rebuilt a full installer for the split.

issues.title: fix(windows): apply exclusion routes transactionally
issues.body:
## Summary

Make Windows WG/AWG exclusion-route installation batched and transactional, and stabilize route reconciliation.

Fixes #3377.
Tracking issue: #3378.

This PR has been narrowed to the Windows route-application portion of the original combined patch. The other parts are now #3379 (AllowedIPs/site allowlist) and #3380 (CIDRs, hostnames and DNS lifecycle).

## Problem

I encountered exclusions remaining visible in settings while their destinations still used the tunnel, and slow/intermittent connectivity with a large exclusion list.

The daemon previously ignored individual exclusion-route installation failures. Activation or server switching could proceed with a partial list. Windows also fetched and scanned the growing route table separately for each prefix, while route notifications could trigger repeated reconciliations.

## Changes

- Introduce a batch exclusion API, with a rollback-capable fallback for non-Windows backends.
- Update daemon reference counts only after the requested additions succeed.
- Roll back additions when activation or server switching fails; propagate installation errors.
- Preserve the previous peer when switching fails and clean up newly installed prefixes.
- Reuse routing-table/interface information for a batch and select the physical route for each exclusion.
- Preserve equivalent pre-existing routes without claiming ownership; clean up only owned routes.
- Deduplicate destinations and skip non-routable entries.
- Debounce route-change bursts, handle notifications without a route row, and avoid retrying the same conflicting captured route within one pass.
- Use type-safe address copies in the Windows route monitor.

The existing large-batch optimization is retained: for batches of at least 500 entries, the code attempts to suspend the process hosting `wcmSvc` while applying routes, then resume it on scope exit. This uses NT process APIs and is process-wide, not a service-only pause. Missing APIs/privileges fall back to ordinary batch installation. This behavior deserves explicit review; it is not a claim that every Windows configuration or failure path has been tested.

## Scope

Seven changed files: the common daemon/batch interface and Windows route-monitor/backend implementation. No hostname/DNS or AllowedIPs parser changes remain in this PR. Application-based split-tunneling behavior and the application version are unchanged.

## Verification

### Previous full-build/live results

- Built the Windows x64 client, service and IFW installer on upstream `94b51df2` (5.0.3.1); the route implementation was used in my local 5.0.3.2 build.
- Earlier checks covered a mixed domain/CIDR exclusion list and disconnect/reconnect behavior.
- A later read-only route audit of that installed build sampled 2,784 addresses, including subnet boundaries, from 1,104 IPv4 exclusions: none selected the VPN interface. Representative excluded HTTPS destinations used the physical interface and a non-excluded control used the tunnel.

### This split

- Based directly on dev `3f6ecacf`.
- `git diff --check` passes.
- All three independent branches merge without conflicts and reconstruct the previous complete patch, apart from moving an unchanged helper in the AllowedIPs sibling.
- No full client/service/installer rebuild was performed after this split. Earlier live checks do not establish every rollback/failure path, IPv6 topology or real application-bypass behavior.

## Related issues and overlapping PRs

- #2248: slow/unstable Windows connection setup with large split-tunneling lists.
- #3020: quadratic per-prefix route setup. The batch path addresses that scaling mechanism; the separately reported access-violation crash has not been proven to share that exact cause.

I reproduced a configuration-generation bug in the desktop WG/AWG path on Windows: **Only the sites listed here will be accessed through the VPN** still produces a full IPv4 tunnel when the profile contains only `0.0.0.0/0`. Reordering the IPv4 and IPv6 defaults has the same effect.

I compiled the actual controller source and captured its activation message through an isolated QLocalServer/QLocalSocket pair. The test does not contact the real VPN service or alter routes.

Input with dummy endpoint information and no credentials:

```json
{
  "protocol": "awg",
  "awg_config_data": {
    "allowed_ips": ["0.0.0.0/0"],
    "hostName": "192.0.2.1"
  },
```

issues.title: Windows site exclusions can be partially applied without failing tunnel activation
issues.body:
## Describe the bug

I encountered CIDR entries remaining visible in my exclusion list while their destinations still used the VPN, together with slow or intermittent connections on a large Windows exclusion list.

This issue tracks the route-application layer separately from hostname resolution and WG/AWG AllowedIPs handling.

At dev `3f6ecacff15e0ada890f6cf5174602d2b6b899c5`, `Daemon::activate()` and `Daemon::switchServer()` add excluded routes one at a time without checking the result. A failed route can therefore leave a partially installed list while activation continues. The route monitor also takes a fresh routing-table snapshot per prefix, and route notifications can repeatedly reconcile an expanding table.

## Reproduction and evidence

1. On Windows, use WG/AWG with site splitting in the all-sites-except-listed mode.
2. Add IPv4/CIDR exclusions, connect, and compare the actual selected interface for excluded destinations with the configured list.
3. A route-installation failure is the relevant failure condition: the current daemon ignores the return value instead of failing and undoing the additions.

The ignored return values and missing batch rollback are source-level findings. My earlier live observations establish incorrectly routed exclusions and slow setup, but I have not performed a fresh failure-injection run on current dev. The scaling reproduction with 12,840 prefixes is independently documented in #3020.

## Expected behavior

- Install an exclusion batch against a reusable physical-route snapshot.
- Commit reference-count changes only after successful installation.
- On activation/server-switch failure, roll back additions and report failure.
- Preserve pre-existing routes that the monitor does not own.
- Reconcile gateway/interface changes without repeated work for each route notification.
- Remove only owned routes during cleanup.

## Environment and scope

Windows x64, WireGuard/AmneziaWG, large IPv4 site-exclusion lists.

The existing combined implementation was built and tested on Windows before this split. A read-only check of my installed patched build found no VPN-selected route among 2,784 sampled addresses from 1,104 exclusions. This is not proof of every failure path, IPv6 configuration or application-based bypass.

The common daemon and the fallback batch API are also touched; Windows-specific route monitoring is the main implementation scope.

- #2248: very slow Windows setup with large split-tunneling lists.
- #3020: per-prefix routing-table work becomes quadratic. This issue also reports a crash whose exact cause is not established; I am not claiming that crash is proven fixed.
- #3021: overlapping batch-route implementation.
- #3375: separate AllowedIPs/site-allowlist failure.

issues.title: Site split-tunneling domain addresses become stale and duplicate imports lose addresses
issues.body:
## Describe the bug

I encountered destinations from my site exclusion list still using the VPN or timing out after connecting or reconnecting. The hostname/CIDR input and stored-address layer needs its own fix, independently of WG/AWG profile eligibility and Windows route installation.

At dev `3f6ecacff15e0ada890f6cf5174602d2b6b899c5`:

- duplicate JSON records with the same hostname overwrite each other's address lists;
- cached hostname addresses are not refreshed before WG/AWG activation/reconnection;
- a DNS lookup started in one route mode can finish after I select another mode and write into the wrong list;
- URL-like input is handled through string replacement rather than URL parsing; invalid CIDR-like input can fall through to hostname/path normalization.

Current dev already preserves basic valid CIDRs and supports multiple stored addresses. This report does not claim those capabilities are entirely absent; it concerns the remaining normalization, import and address-lifecycle gaps.

## Minimal import reproduction

Import the following into site split tunneling:

```json
[
  {"hostname":"example.com","ips":["198.51.100.10"]},
  {"hostname":"example.com","ips":["198.51.100.20"]}
]
```

Expected: one hostname retaining both unique addresses.
Actual in the current import loop: the later `sites.insert(normalizedHostname, ips)` replaces the earlier address list.

These are documentation-only addresses; the reproduction concerns stored data, not connectivity to them.

For the DNS lifecycle, a domain's stored address can become stale between connections. Reconnecting should refresh successfully resolved addresses while preserving the last known addresses on DNS failure. An in-flight lookup must remain associated with the list in which it started and must not resurrect a deleted entry.

## Expected behavior

- Validate IPv4/CIDR entries before URL normalization; preserve valid prefixes and reject malformed ones.
- Parse URLs/hostnames consistently, including case, IDNs and trailing dots.
- Merge duplicate imported hostnames without losing addresses, retaining legacy single-IP compatibility.
- Refresh WG/AWG domain entries before connection, with bounded concurrency, timeout and cancellation.
- Refresh on reconnect and ignore obsolete lookup results; do not multiply reconnect callbacks.

## Environment and verification limits

I originally encountered the problem on Windows with WG/AWG, public services with multiple IPv4 addresses, and a private hostname resolved through hosts. The existing combined patch was built and exercised on Windows; it is now being separated for review on current dev.

The normalization/storage code is shared. Pre-connect resolution in this patch is desktop WG/AWG-only and IPv4-only. It does not add wildcard-domain routing, continuous DNS monitoring, or prove the behavior of every mobile platform.

## Related work

- #2939 describes the earlier CIDR-prefix loss during import; basic preservation is already in current dev.
- #2825 overlaps multi-address hostname/pre-connect resolution.
- #3018 overlaps CIDR import regression coverage.
- #3375 tracks the independent WG/AWG AllowedIPs eligibility/serialization problem.

Fix: #3380. Umbrella tracker: #3378. The sibling fixes are #3379 (AllowedIPs) and #3030 (Windows routes).

issues.title: macOS: NAT64-synthesized IPv6 endpoint passed to wireguard-go without brackets → IPC error -22, AmneziaWG can't connect (DNS64 networks)
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**
On macOS, when an AmneziaWG server is added by **hostname** (A record only, no AAAA) and the Mac is on a network with **DNS64/NAT64** (e.g. mobile hotspot of a Russian mobile operator), the hostname resolves to a NAT64-synthesized address `64:ff9b::/96`. The macOS daemon then passes it to wireguard-go as `endpoint=<ipv6>:<port>` **without square brackets**, wireguard-go rejects it with IPC error -22, peer creation fails and the connection is immediately dropped (the GUI may sit in "Preparing"/"Connecting").

The same server added by **IPv4 literal** works on the same network. Android client works with the hostname on the same network. Same root cause as the Linux issue #2607, but on macOS and triggered by NAT64 synthesis rather than a real AAAA record.

**Root cause (from source, dev @ 7f9b7db)**
`client/platforms/macos/daemon/wireguardutilsmacos.cpp`, `WireguardUtilsMacos::updatePeer()`:
```cpp
if (!config.m_serverIpv4AddrIn.isNull()) {
    out << "endpoint=" << config.m_serverIpv4AddrIn << ":";      // <- holds 64:ff9b::… here, no brackets
} else if (!config.m_serverIpv6AddrIn.isNull()) {
    out << "endpoint=[" << config.m_serverIpv6AddrIn << "]:";
```
The resolved hostname result ends up in `m_serverIpv4AddrIn` even when it is an IPv6 (NAT64) address. Suggested fix: bracket the address whenever it contains `:` (or put IPv6 results into `m_serverIpv6AddrIn`), and/or prefer A records when resolving the endpoint host.

**To Reproduce**
1. Add a self-hosted AmneziaWG server by hostname that has only an A record (e.g. `relay.example.net` → `203.0.113.10`).
2. Connect the Mac to a DNS64/NAT64 network (mobile hotspot).
3. Click Connect → immediately disconnected.

**Service log** (`/private/var/log/AmneziaVPN/AmneziaVPN-service.log`, key/addresses anonymized)
```
MacosRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for 64:ff9b::cb00:710a/128
WireguardUtilsMacos : Configuring peer <pubkey> via 64:ff9b::cb00:710a
WireguardGo : ERROR: (utun4) IPC error -22: failed to set endpoint 64:ff9b::cb00:710a:5275: invalid ip:port "64:ff9b::cb00:710a:5275", IPv6 addresses must be surrounded by square brackets
WireguardUtilsMacos : Peer configuration failed: Unknown error: -22
Daemon : Peer creation failed.
DaemonLocalServerConnection : Failed to activate the interface
```

**Expected behavior**
Connection succeeds (bracketed endpoint `[64:ff9b::cb00:710a]:5275`), or the client uses the A record.

**Environment**
- AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0 (de93650), macOS Sequoia 15.7.5 (x86_64)
- Protocol: AmneziaWG, self-hosted server added via hostname

issues.title: fix: cover CVE-2026-98432
Android: auto-reconnect when the AmneziaWG tunnel stalls after idle (connection watchdog)
issues.body:
AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.1 (AWG 3.1), Android 16, OnePlus 15.
Self-hosted AmneziaWG, mobile network (Russia), battery set
to "Unrestricted" for AmneziaVPN.

Problem
After the phone has been idle with the screen off, the tunnel
sometimes stalls: nothing works (Telegram, browser) until I
manually disconnect and reconnect in AmneziaVPN. It happens
several times a day. A manual reconnect always fixes it
immediately.

What we see on the server side
We captured traffic on our server during these episodes. While
the tunnel is stalled, no packets from the phone reach the server
at all — no handshake initiation, nothing, for 4–44 minutes.
Other devices on the same server work normally at the same time.
Typical sequence: the phone wakes up, sends a few data packets
with the old session from a new NAT port (the mobile operator
changed it during sleep), the server drops them (keys older than
180 s), and then the phone never sends a new handshake. A manual
reconnect opens a new socket, the handshake completes in ~0.1 s,
and traffic flows right away.

Feature request: connection watchdog
An option to detect a stalled tunnel and restart it automatically,
for example:
- if the latest handshake is older than ~140 s
  (REKEY_AFTER_TIME + KEEPALIVE_TIMEOUT + REKEY_TIMEOUT, as in
  wireguard-tools reresolve-dns) while the app has traffic to send,
  or
- if a periodic check through the tunnel (ping/HTTP) fails
  N times in a row,
then recreate the socket and re-handshake — the same as a manual
reconnect. Configurable interval and on/off switch.

Similar features exist in other clients: WG Tunnel ("Restart
tunnel on ping failure"), mihomo-based clients (fallback groups
with health checks).

Server-side keepalive does not help here: we tried
PersistentKeepalive 25 on the server for this peer — the server
cannot reach the phone after the operator's NAT mapping changes,
only the phone can recover by sending first.

Thank you for AmneziaVPN!

issues.title: feat(split-tunneling): support live IPv4 rule additions for WG/AWG
issues.body:
### Problem and current scope

Adding a split tunneling address currently requires disconnecting and reconnecting the VPN. This draft introduces live IPv4 address/subnet additions for eligible WG/AWG connections, without an automatic reconnect fallback.

Both routing modes are covered: add destinations **via VPN**, or add destinations **directly** outside the tunnel. Split tunneling must already be enabled. Removal, clearing/replacing the list, changing its mode and enabling/disabling split tunneling remain unavailable while connected. Existing empty-list semantics are preserved.

### Architecture and safety changes

A coordinator receives a platform backend through constructor injection. It serializes/coalesces requests, binds them to the active session and tracks pending/applied configurations separately. Results are explicit: `Applied`, `NotApplied` after confirmed compensation, or `StateUnknown`. Unknown outcomes block further live editing; unsupported connections keep the existing restrictions.

The desktop service updates the current interface and compensates failed operations:

- Linux replaces the split firewall chains in one checked `iptables-restore` transaction. macOS replaces PF anchors in a protection-preserving order. The hot path is separate from startup configuration, and no firewall commands are issued when KillSwitch is disabled.
- Route creation returns an ownership receipt. Conflicts are rejected without overwriting pre-existing routes; rollback removes only resources created by that request, including partial default-route creation. Linux waits for kernel netlink ACKs and remembers the gateway used for an exclusion.
- Windows propagates route failures and retains failed cleanup records for retry. WFP rules use transactions. An unknown-state latch is cleared only after verified cleanup commits, rather than merely on a reconnect request. Queued network notifications cannot recreate routes after cleanup starts.

These changes are in `ff9054d8`; passing tests does not establish leak-free behavior on every OS.

### Apple dependency and integration

**Depends on the library Draft PR: https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amneziawg-apple/pull/53.**

Client integration: https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/commit/ee9875fad586337e29d6b1be7892d16c1c9524be.

The previous unverified Apple bridge was removed. The new bridge uses the library's routing-only contract, preserving the running peer instead of calling its general peer-replacing update. It checks request/session IDs, public key, mode and IPv4 additions; stale/duplicate responses cannot update another session. Profile settings are persisted after the tunnel confirms application; failed persistence is treated as unknown.

**Apple live routing remains disabled by default** behind `AMNEZIA_ENABLE_APPLE_LIVE_ROUTING`. Its build requires matching Swift sources and a target-SDK Go archive; the vendor submodule is unchanged while the library PR is reviewed. The source lists also preserve the build path with the old dependency when this capability is off.

For this Apple draft, only an existing inclusion/exclusion session is eligible. The effective mode-0/full-tunnel transition used by an empty list remains excluded until its `includeAllNetworks` policy is validated. That is separate from desktop coverage and is not a change to empty-list semantics.

### Platform coverage and evidence

| Backend | Current state | Available verification |
|---|---|---|
| Windows desktop | Eligible WG/AWG additions implemented | Transaction tests and actual route-monitor tests with simulated SDK/WinAPI; native Windows/WFP traffic validation pending |
| Linux desktop | Eligible WG/AWG additions implemented | Real kernel route/permission probes and nft/legacy firewall updates in isolated network namespaces; complete application/device matrix pending |
| macOS desktop service | Eligible WG/AWG additions implemented | Universal service build, focused tests and PF syntax checks; prior macOS

comments.body:
I can confirm a very similar **shared-config DNS failure on Linux**, specifically **Pop!_OS 24.04 LTS (COSMIC), AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0 (`de93650`), Xray**.

The VPN connection was originally created on a phone and then imported to the Linux laptop using **Share connection**. It displayed **Connected**, and HTTPS through the tunnel worked when bypassing DNS (`curl --resolve` returned `HTTP/2 200`), but ordinary DNS requests timed out and websites would not load.

Diagnostics:

- `resolvectl status tun2` showed `172.29.172.254` as the resolver despite setting `1.1.1.1` and `1.0.0.1` in the client.
- `resolvectl query -4 example.com` timed out.
- Local Xray repeatedly logged `accepted udp:172.29.172.254:53` (and also TCP/53), with no DNS response observed.
- The Amnezia firewall's `amnvpn.320.allowDNS` ACCEPT counters increased on `tun2` during lookups (UDP/53: 14 -> 34 packets; TCP/53: 0 -> 32), while `amnvpn.310.blockDNS` and `amnvpn.100.blockAll` counters remained at 0. That shows DNS requests were allowed by those local rules, not where the replies were lost.
- With VPN disconnected, `resolvectl query example.com` succeeded in ~31 ms.

**Confirmed fix:** On the phone, I **disabled AmneziaDNS, generated a new sharing link, and imported that new configuration into Linux**. This immediately fixed the DNS issue. The new `resolvectl status tun2` showed:

```text
Current DNS Server: 1.0.0.1
DNS Servers: 1.1.1.1 1.0.0.1
DNS Domain: ~.
```

`resolvectl query -4 example.com` succeeded in ~290 ms, and a normal `curl -4 -I --noproxy '*' https://example.com` returned `HTTP/2 200`.

This suggests that the issue with DNS information embedded in a shared Xray configuration / client DNS handling also affects **Linux**, not only Windows. The exact point where traffic to the private DNS destination is lost was **not conclusively proven** in my Linux test.

comments.issue_title: feat(split-tunneling): wildcard site entries, resolved by observing DNS
comments.body:
Worth flagging for whoever picks this up: #3383 was opened twenty minutes after this one and covers the same ground from a different direction. The two touch 13 of the same files, so they cannot both be merged as they stand.

The approaches differ in kind, not only in detail:

- This PR observes the tunnel's DNS and installs address-based exclusion routes through the daemon's existing `addExclusionRoute` path. Being address-based, it exempts an unrelated service that happens to share a CDN address with a matched one. That limit is stated in the description and no amount of parsing removes it.
- #3383 runs the bundled Xray locally as a TUN with FakeDNS and matches HTTP Host / TLS SNI, which does distinguish services behind a shared address. It is Windows-only and opt-in, disabled by default.

They also disagree on something user-visible: here `*.example.com` covers `example.com` as well as everything below it; in #3383 the apex is deliberately not covered.

I am happy to defer to #3383, or to rework this on top of it, whichever is more useful. If an address-based path is still wanted for the platforms #3383 does not cover, the daemon-side pieces here are independent of how names are matched and could be reused on their own: the route table that expires a learned address with the TTL that justified it and caps how many one pattern can create, and the firewall permits installed and withdrawn in the same operation as the route, without which the kill switch drops the traffic the route was meant to let out.

One caveat repeated from the description, since it bears on reviewing either PR: only the Windows build is compiled and tested here. The Linux and macOS files mirror the Windows implementation and have not been built. The workflows in this repository trigger on `push` rather than on `pull_request`, so CI does not build fork pull requests either, and Codacy is the only check that runs.

comments.body:
**Validation update — macOS desktop r3 / arm64 / AmneziaWG**

**Checked:** live additions in both routing modes, the first exclusion from an empty list, and a domain addition using the existing one-shot IPv4 resolver. Routes and HTTPS behaved as expected; persistent TCP/TLS connections survived additions without restarting the backend. Five focused client CTest suites passed.

With KillSwitch enabled, a controlled backend pause interrupted protected HTTPS while excluded HTTPS remained available. Protected connectivity recovered after resuming the same backend. This test preserved TUN/routes and does not establish leak-free behavior.

**Still unverified:** full native Windows/Linux VPN runs, a separate WireGuard run, signed Apple Network Extension apps, native CIDR/overlap cases, comprehensive UDP/IPv6 coverage, sleep/network changes, and packet capture during updates and failures.

**Implementation status:** the current approach is functional in the tested scenarios. However, desktop updates on Windows/Linux/macOS clear and rebuild AllowedIPs, potentially causing brief packet drops. These drops were not measured in the current tests.

The proposed refinement is to preserve unchanged peer settings and apply prefix differences with checked rollback. Full-tunnel transitions need separate handling. Apple routing remains default-OFF; two local NE CMake header-path fixes still need to be included in the PR.
